fields.subtitle: Devarim, “Words”
fields.description: The fifth book of the Bible, called in Hebrew Devarim from its opening, “These are the words Moses spoke to all Israel”: Moses’ farewell to a new generation on the plains of Moab, with the promised land in sight across the Jordan and his own death near. He retells the forty years, gives the Ten Commandments again, and sets at the heart of everything the Shema, “Hear, Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one”, with the command to love God with the whole heart. Then laws for life in the land, with open hands for the poor and justice for the outsider, the fatherless and the widow; a prophet promised like Moses; blessing and curse; the call to choose life; the song of the Rock; and Moses on Mount Nebo, seeing the land he will not enter. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Deuteronomy?
qa.answer: The fifth and last of the five books of Moses. Its Hebrew name, Devarim, “Words”, comes from its opening line; the name Deuteronomy, Greek for “second law”, comes from the Greek translation of “a copy of this law” in 17:18. It is made mainly of Moses’ farewell speeches to Israel on the plains of Moab: a retelling of the journey (chapters 1–4), the commandments and laws for life in the land (5–26), blessings and curses and the covenant renewed (27–30), and Moses’ last days and death (31–34). It is the law of Sinai preached again to a new generation.

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Deuteronomy?
qa.answer: The book says that Moses spoke these words and wrote down “this law” (31:9, 24), and Jewish and Christian tradition has received it as his, with the account of his death in chapter 34 long read as added by another hand. Many scholars connect it instead with “the book of the law” found in the temple in King Josiah’s reign, in 622 BC, whose reforms follow its laws closely (2 Kings 22–23), and think it was completed later still. Others hold that it preserves Moses’ own covenant, shaped for later generations. Christians hold a range of views on these questions.

qa.question: What is the Shema?
qa.answer: The words of Deuteronomy 6:4–9, named from their first word in Hebrew, “Hear”: “Hear, Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. You are to love the LORD your God with your whole heart, with your whole being, and with all your strength.” Jewish prayer has recited them morning and evening for many centuries, and Jesus gave them when he was asked for the greatest commandment (Mark 12:29–30). The Hebrew of 6:4 can be read in more than one way, as “the LORD is one” or “the LORD alone”, and both readings confess that Israel’s God is the only God.

qa.question: Why was Moses not allowed to enter the promised land?
qa.answer: Because at the waters of Meribah, when the people quarreled with him for lack of water, Moses struck the rock instead of speaking to it, and God said that he and Aaron had not trusted him or shown his holiness before the people (Numbers 20:10–12; Deuteronomy 32:51). Moses pleaded to be allowed across (Deuteronomy 3:23–26), but was told only to look at the land from the summit of Pisgah. He died on Mount Nebo, and the book says that no one knows where his grave is (34:6). In the Gospels he appears in the land at last, talking with Jesus on the mountain of the transfiguration.

qa.question: Who is the prophet like Moses in Deuteronomy 18?
qa.answer: Moses tells Israel, “The LORD your God will raise up a prophet for you like me, one of your own fellow Israelites from among you. It is to him you must listen” (18:15). The words can be read of the true prophets who followed Moses one after another. But the book’s last chapter says that no prophet like Moses had arisen (34:10), and by the time of Jesus many were waiting for “the Prophet”. In Acts 3:22 Peter says that Jesus is the one Moses meant.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Hear, Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. You are to love the LORD your God with your whole heart, with your whole being, and with all your strength.

— Deuteronomy 6:4–5

Deuteronomy is the last will and testament of Moses. Forty years after the exodus, Israel is camped on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from the land God promised. Moses is a hundred and twenty years old, and he knows he will not cross the river with them. So he gathers the people one last time, and he preaches. The book is made almost entirely of his words, and in Hebrew it is named after them: Devarim, “Words”, from its opening, “These are the words Moses spoke to all Israel”.

The name we use comes from the ancient Greek translation and means “second law”. It arose from a verse in chapter 17, where the king is told to write out “a copy of this law”, which the Greek rendered as “this second law”. The name is not quite right, because Deuteronomy is not a new law. But it is not quite wrong either. It is the law of Sinai preached a second time, to a new generation, on the edge of a new life.

Few books of the Old Testament mattered more to Jesus. When the devil tempted him in the wilderness, he answered three times from Deuteronomy. When he was asked for the greatest commandment, he quoted Deuteronomy 6. And for centuries Jewish men and women have said its central words every morning and every evening: “Hear, Israel.”

The shape of the book

Deuteronomy is built mainly from three speeches of Moses, followed by an account of his last days:

  • the first speech: remembering the journey from Horeb to Moab (chapters 1–4)
  • the second speech: the commandments (5–11), the laws for life in the land (12–26), and the blessings and curses (27–28)
  • the third speech: the covenant renewed in Moab, and the call to choose life (29–30)
  • Moses’ last days: Joshua appointed, the song of Moses, the blessing of the tribes, and his death on Mount Nebo (31–34)

Many scholars have noticed that this shape resembles the treaties that ancient kings made with their subject peoples: a history of what the great king has done, the obligations of the people, blessings and curses, witnesses, and arrangements for the treaty to be kept and read. Deuteronomy is a covenant document. But it is a covenant preached with tears, by a pastor who loves his people and fears for them.

“Remember”

The first speech is a retelling. Moses goes back over the forty years: the appointment of judges, the scouts and the refusal at Kadesh, the long years of wandering, and the first victories east of the Jordan. Most of the people listening were children when those things happened, or not yet born. Moses insists that the story is theirs anyway:

The LORD did not make this covenant with our fathers; he made it with us, the ones here today, all of us still alive.

— Deuteronomy 5:3

Two words run all through the book: “remember” and “do not forget”. Israel is to remember that they were slaves in Egypt, remember the wilderness, remember what their own eyes have seen, and tell it to their children. Moses reminds them how God carried them in the wilderness “as a father carries his son”, and he asks a question that could only be asked of Israel:

For what great nation has gods as near to it as the LORD our God is to us whenever we call to him? And what great nation has statutes and rulings as righteous as this whole law that I put before you today?

— Deuteronomy 4:7–8

The great lesson of the history is that there is only one God. “So know this today, and take it to heart: the LORD is God in the heavens above and on the earth below, and there is no other.” Moses also warns them that if they turn to idols in the land, they will be scattered among the nations. Yet even there, he says, “you will seek the LORD your God, and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.”

“Hear, Israel”

The second speech begins with the Ten Commandments, spoken again. They are almost the same as in Exodus 20, but one difference is telling. In Exodus the Sabbath is grounded in creation. Here it is grounded in rescue:

Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God led you out from there by a strong hand and an outstretched arm. For this reason the LORD your God has commanded you to observe the Sabbath day.

— Deuteronomy 5:15

Then comes the Shema, named from its first word, “Hear”: the words at the head of this introduction. The LORD is one, and he is to be loved with the whole heart, the whole being and all one’s strength. It is a command to love, which is a strange thing to command. But Deuteronomy believes that love is something you do as well as feel: something you keep, teach and practise. So Moses goes on at once to the everyday means of keeping it:

Keep these words that I am commanding you today close to your heart. Teach them carefully to your children, and speak of them as you sit in your house and as you go on your way, as you lie down and as you rise.

— Deuteronomy 6:6–7

The words are to be tied on the hand and written on the doorposts, and many Jewish homes still fix a small case containing them to the doorframe. Faith in Deuteronomy is passed on at the kitchen table and along the road, by parents who answer their children’s questions. “Some day your son will ask you, ‘What do they mean, these decrees, statutes and rulings that the LORD our God has commanded you?’” And the answer begins not with a rule but with a story: “In Egypt we were slaves to Pharaoh.”

Chosen in love

Why Israel? Deuteronomy answers with disarming honesty. Not because they were great, and not because they were good:

The LORD gave his heart to you and chose you, not because there were more of you than of any other people, for you were the smallest of all the peoples, but because the LORD loved you and would not break the oath he swore to your ancestors. So he led you out by his strong hand and bought you free from the house where you were slaves, out of the grip of Pharaoh king of Egypt.

— Deuteronomy 7:7–8

God loved them because he loved them. Two chapters later Moses makes the same point about the land: “it is not because you are righteous that the LORD your God is giving you this good land to possess, for you are a stiff-necked people.” Grace comes first in Deuteronomy, as it does in Exodus. The commandments are the grateful response of a people who have been loved.

“Do not forget”

Moses knows that the greatest danger lies not in the wilderness but in the land, when life becomes easy. The wilderness years were meant to teach dependence:

He brought you low and let you go hungry, then gave you manna to eat, a food that neither you nor your ancestors had ever known. He did this to teach you that people do not live on bread alone, but people live on everything that comes from the mouth of the LORD.

— Deuteronomy 8:3

In the land there will be fine houses, growing herds and silver and gold, and the temptation will be to say, “My own power and the strength of my own hands have won me this wealth.” Moses answers, “Remember the LORD your God instead. It is he who gives you the ability to grow wealthy.” It is one of the most searching warnings in the Bible for anyone who has prospered.

And then, in chapter 10, Moses gathers it all into a single question:

And now, Israel, what is it that the LORD your God asks of you? Just this: that you fear the LORD your God, follow all his ways and love him, and that you serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and that you keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD that I am giving you today, for your own good.

— Deuteronomy 10:12–13

The God who owns the highest heavens “sees that orphans and widows get justice, and he loves the outsider”. So must Israel: “You too must love the outsider, since you were outsiders yourselves in the land of Egypt.” Moses even asks for something no law can produce: “Circumcise your hearts, then, and stop stiffening your necks.”

Laws for life in the land

Chapters 12–26 set out the laws by which Israel is to live. They begin with worship: sacrifice is to be brought not anywhere but to “the place that the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name there”. Then come festivals and tithes, judges, kings, priests and prophets, war, family life, and the treatment of neighbours, workers, animals and the poor.

Running through them is a passion for justice and generosity. “Pursue what is right, nothing but what is right.” The poor are not to be met with a closed hand: “open your hand to him generously and lend him as much as he needs to meet his want.” At harvest, a forgotten sheaf is to be left “to the outsider, the fatherless child and the widow”. Even the ox treading grain is not to be muzzled. And again and again the reason is the same: “Remember that you were slaves in Egypt.”

The king, too, stands under the law. He must not pile up horses, wives or gold, and he must write out his own copy of the law and read it all his life, “so that he does not think himself above his fellow Israelites.” And Moses promises a successor of a different kind:

The LORD your God will raise up a prophet for you like me, one of your own fellow Israelites from among you. It is to him you must listen.

— Deuteronomy 18:15

The words can be read of the line of true prophets who would follow Moses. But the last chapter says that no prophet like him had yet arisen, and by the time of Jesus many were waiting for “the Prophet”. Peter, preaching in the temple, says plainly that Jesus is the one Moses meant (Acts 3:22).

Some of these laws are hard for modern readers, above all the commands to devote the nations of Canaan “wholly to destruction”. Christians have wrestled with them in different ways: as a unique judgment on peoples whose wickedness the book describes, limited to one time and place; as the language of ancient warfare, not always meant literally; or as a hard part of a story that finds its answer only in the cross. The book’s own stated reason is that Israel should not learn to copy the practices of those nations. It is right to read these chapters soberly, and not to pretend they are easy.

The laws end with a liturgy. When an Israelite brings the first fruits of the harvest, he is to recite the story of his people, beginning, “My ancestor was an Aramean, a wanderer”, and ending with thanksgiving for “a land that flows with milk and honey.” Then he is to rejoice, with the Levite and the outsider beside him.

Blessing and curse, life and death

Chapters 27–28 set out the blessings that will follow faithfulness and the curses that will follow rebellion. Six tribes are to stand on Mount Gerizim for the blessing, six on Mount Ebal for the curse. The curses are long and terrible, and they end in exile. But chapter 30 looks beyond exile to a return, and to a change that only God can make:

The LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the hearts of your descendants, so that you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and so live.

— Deuteronomy 30:6

What Moses commanded in chapter 10, God here promises to do. Jeremiah and Ezekiel would take up the same hope, of a new heart and a new covenant. And Moses insists that God’s word is not far away or beyond reach:

No, the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, for you to do.

— Deuteronomy 30:14

Paul quotes these words in Romans 10 and applies them to the gospel of Christ, “the message of faith that we proclaim.” And then Moses sets the choice before them, heaven and earth as witnesses: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. So choose life, that you and your descendants may live”.

Moses’ last days

The last chapters gather up Moses’ final acts. He commissions Joshua: “Be strong and courageous.” He writes down the law and orders it to be read aloud to all Israel every seven years, “men, women and children, and the outsiders who live in your towns”. He teaches the people a song, in which God is “The Rock: his work is perfect”, and Israel is the child he found in the desert, guarded “as the pupil of his eye”, carried like an eagle’s young. He blesses the tribes one by one, and ends with a promise: “The God of old is a refuge, and underneath are arms that last forever.”

It is a hard ending for the man who had carried this people for forty years. Early in the book Moses tells how he begged to cross: “Please let me go across and see the good land on the far side of the Jordan.” The answer was no, and at the end God names the reason: Moses had broken faith with him at the waters of Meribah. He does not hide his grief, but he does not let it sour his last words, which are all blessing.

Then he climbs Mount Nebo, and God shows him the whole land, and he dies there in the land of Moab. Someone, perhaps God himself, buries him, and no one knows where. The book’s last words are his epitaph:

Never again has Israel had a prophet like Moses, one the LORD knew face to face, none like him in all the signs and wonders the LORD sent him to do in the land of Egypt, against Pharaoh, all his officials and his whole land, and in all the mighty power and all the great and terrifying deeds that Moses did in the sight of all Israel.

— Deuteronomy 34:10–12

How to read Deuteronomy

Read it aloud if you can. It is a book of sermons, and its long sentences and repetitions are the rhythms of a preacher. Read it after Numbers, so that you hear it as Moses’ people did, a generation whose parents had died in the wilderness. And read it with the New Testament open, because it is one of the books the New Testament quotes most often.

Listen for the words the book repeats. “Today” occurs again and again: the covenant is not a memory but a choice to be made now, by whoever is hearing. The phrase “with all your heart and with all your soul” runs through the book like a refrain. The phrase “the place that the LORD your God will choose” looks forward to a sanctuary not yet named, which later books will find in Jerusalem. And “the outsider, the fatherless child and the widow” keep appearing together, as though Moses cannot speak of the land’s harvest without thinking of those who own none of it.

It helps, too, to notice how much of the rest of the Old Testament is written in Deuteronomy’s accent. The books from Joshua to Kings measure Israel’s kings by its standards; of Josiah the writer says that he turned to the LORD “with his whole heart, with his whole being, and with all his strength”, the very words of the Shema. The prophets call Israel back to its covenant and threaten its curses. And when the exiles prayed for a way home, they could lean on its promise that even from the farthest edge of the sky, God would gather them.

The book says that Moses spoke these words and wrote down “this law” (31:9, 24), and Jewish and Christian tradition has received it as his; its account of his death has long been read as added by another hand. Many scholars connect it instead with “the book of the law” found in the temple in King Josiah’s reign, in 622 BC, whose reforms follow its laws closely (2 Kings 22–23), and think it was completed later still. Others hold that it preserves Moses’ own covenant, shaped for later generations. Christians hold a range of views on these questions, while hearing in it the voice of God to his people.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Deuteronomy are worth knowing before you begin.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, the four letters often written Yahweh, this translation follows long Jewish and Christian custom and writes “the LORD”.

The Shema. The Hebrew of 6:4 has no verbs and can be read in more than one way. The translation keeps close to it: “Hear, Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.” In 6:5 the word often rendered “soul” is “your whole being”, the whole living person.

“Faithful love.” The Hebrew hesed, God’s covenant love, is “faithful love”: God “keeps his covenant and his faithful love for a thousand generations”.

“The outsider.” The foreigner who lives among Israel, whom the book so often names beside the widow and the fatherless, is usually “the outsider”.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Deuteronomy 1
fields.body_html:
The words Moses spoke across the Jordan

These are the words Moses spoke to all Israel in the wilderness across the Jordan: in the Arabah facing Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth and Di-zahab. It is eleven days’ journey from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea by the Mount Seir road. On the first day of the eleventh month, in the fortieth year, Moses spoke to the Israelites and told them everything that the LORD had commanded him to give them. This was after he had defeated Sihon king of the Amorites, whose city was Heshbon, and Og king of Bashan, whose cities were Ashtaroth and Edrei. Across the Jordan in the land of Moab, Moses set about explaining this law. He said, “The LORD our God spoke to us at Horeb and said, ‘Your time at this mountain has been long enough. Turn and move on. Go into the hill country of the Amorites and to all the regions near it: the Arabah, the hill country, the foothills, the Negev and the seacoast, the land of the Canaanites, and Lebanon, as far as the great river, the Euphrates. Look, I have placed the land in front of you. Go in and take possession of the land that the LORD swore to give to your ancestors Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and to their descendants after them.’ Back then I told you, ‘Carrying all of you on my own is more than I can do. The LORD your God has increased your numbers, and look at you today: as many as the stars in the sky. May the LORD, the God of your ancestors, increase you a thousandfold beyond what you are now, and bless you as he promised! How am I to carry on my own all your troubles, the load you put on me, and your quarrels? From your tribes, pick men who are wise, discerning and well known, and I will put them at your head.’ You answered me, ‘Your plan is a good one; let it be done.’ So I took the leading men of your tribes, wise and respected men, and set them over you as leaders: commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens, and officials for each of your tribes. At that time I gave your judges this charge: ‘Hear the disputes among your fellow Israelites, and judge fairly in every case, whether it is between two Israelites or between an Israelite and a outsider living among you. In giving judgment, do not take anyone’s side because of who they are. Give the humble and the powerful the same hearing. Fear no one, since the judgment is God’s. If a case is too difficult for you, bring it to me and I will hear it.’ At that time I gave you instructions about everything you were to do. We left Horeb and made our way through that whole vast and fearsome wilderness you have seen, along the road to the hill country of the Amorites, as the LORD our God had commanded us, and we came to Kadesh-barnea. I told you, ‘Now you are at the hill country of the Amorites, the land the LORD our God is giving us. Look, the LORD your God has placed the land before you. Go up and take possession of it, as the LORD, the God of your ancestors, told you. Do not be afraid or lose heart.’ Then you all came to me and said, ‘Let us send men on ahead to explore the land for us. They can come back and tell us which way to go up and what towns we will meet.’ I agreed with the plan, and I chose twelve of your men, one from each tribe. They set out and went up into the hill country, came to the Valley of Eshcol, and explored it. They took some of the land’s fruit with them and brought it down to us. And they gave us their report: ‘The land that the LORD our God is giving us is good.’ But you refused to go up, and set yourselves against the command of the LORD your God. You complained in your tents and said, ‘The LORD hates us. That is why he brought us out of Egypt: to hand us over to the Amorites to wipe us out. Where are we going up to? Our brothers have made us lose heart. They say, “The people are bigger and taller than we are, the cities are large, with walls up to the sky, and we even saw the descendants of the Anakim there.”‘ Then I said to you, ‘Do not tremble; do not be afraid of them. The LORD your God, who goes ahead of you, is the one who will fight for you, as you saw him do for you in Egypt, and in the wilderness. There you saw how the LORD your God carried you the whole way you traveled, as a father carries his son, until you arrived here.’ Yet for all this you did not trust the LORD your God, who went ahead of you on the way to look for places for you to camp, in fire by night to show you which way to go, and in the cloud by day. When the LORD heard what you said, he was angry and swore an oath: ‘Of these men, this evil generation, not a single one will see the good land that I swore I would give your ancestors, except Caleb son of Jephunneh. He will see it, and I will give him and his descendants the land he walked on, because he followed the LORD wholeheartedly.’ Because of you the LORD was angry with me too, and said, ‘You will not go in there either. Joshua son of Nun, your assistant, is the one who will go in. Encourage him, because he will lead Israel to take the land as their inheritance. And your little ones, whom you said would be carried off as plunder, and your children, who today cannot yet tell good from evil, they are the ones who will go in. I will give the land to them, and they will take possession of it. But as for you, turn around and set out into the wilderness along the road to the Red Sea.’ Then you replied to me, ‘We have sinned against the LORD. We will go up and fight, as the LORD our God commanded us.’ So each of you strapped on his weapons, thinking it would be easy to go up into the hill country. But the LORD said to me, ‘Tell them, “Do not go up, and do not fight. I am not among you, and if you go, your enemies will strike you down.”‘ I warned you, but you paid no attention. You set yourselves against the command of the LORD and in your pride went up into the hill country. The Amorites who lived in that hill country came out against you and chased you like a swarm of bees. They cut you down in Seir, all the way to Hormah. Then you came back and wept before the LORD, but the LORD would not listen to your cry or pay any attention to you. So you stayed at Kadesh for a long time, all the time that you stayed there.

fields.title: Deuteronomy 2
fields.body_html:
Passing by Edom, Moab and Ammon

So we turned back and headed into the wilderness by the Red Sea road, as the LORD had told me, and we spent a long time going around the hill country of Seir.

Then the LORD said to me, ‘Your circling of this hill country has gone on long enough. Turn north now. And tell the people: “You are going to cross the land of your relatives, the descendants of Esau, who live in Seir. They will fear you, and you must take great care. Do not start a fight with them, because I will not give you any of their land, not even room enough to set your foot on. I have given the hill country of Seir to Esau as his possession. You are to buy food from them with money so that you can eat, and you are to pay them money for water to drink as well. The LORD your God has blessed all that your hands have done. He has cared for you as you made your way through this great wilderness. The LORD your God has been with you for these forty years, and you have never gone without anything.”‘ So we moved on past our relatives, the descendants of Esau who live in Seir, leaving the road through the Arabah that comes up from Elath and Ezion-geber. Then we turned and went along the road through the wilderness of Moab. Then the LORD said to me, ‘Do not treat Moab as an enemy or start a war with them. I will not give you any of their land to possess, because I have given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their own.’ (In earlier times the Emim lived there, a great people, numerous and as tall as the Anakim. They were reckoned as Rephaim, as the Anakim were, though the Moabites’ name for them is Emim. Seir, too, was once the home of the Horites. The descendants of Esau took it from them, wiping them out as they advanced and settling in their place, just as Israel did in the land that the LORD gave it to possess.) ‘Rise now and cross over the Zered Valley.’ So we crossed over the Zered Valley. The time from when we left Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the Zered Valley was thirty-eight years. That was how long it took for the whole generation of fighting men to die out from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them. Indeed, the hand of the LORD was against them, sweeping them out of the camp until none of them were left. When every one of the fighting men had died and was gone from among the people,

the LORD said to me, ‘Today you are going to cross the border of Moab at Ar. When you come close to the Ammonites, do not treat them as enemies or start a fight with them, for I will not give you any of the Ammonites’ land to possess. I have given it to the descendants of Lot as their own.’ (That land too was counted as a land of the Rephaim. The Rephaim used to live there, though the Ammonites call them Zamzummim, a great people, numerous and as tall as the Anakim. The LORD wiped them out to make way for the Ammonites, who took over their land and settled there in their place, just as he had done for the descendants of Esau who live in Seir, when he wiped out the Horites before them, so that they took over the Horites’ land and live there still, to this day. The Avvites, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, were wiped out by the Caphtorim, who came from Caphtor and settled where the Avvites had been.) ‘Get up, set out, and cross the Arnon Valley. Look, I have handed Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, over to you, and his land with him. Start taking his land, and make war on him. Starting today I will make the peoples everywhere under heaven dread you and fear you. When they hear reports about you, they will tremble and shake with terror because of you.’ Then I sent messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth to Sihon king of Heshbon with an offer of peace: ‘Let me pass through your land. I will keep strictly to the road and will not turn off to the right or the left. Sell me food for money so that I can eat, and give me water for money so that I can drink. Just let me pass through on foot, as the descendants of Esau who live in Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for me, until I cross the Jordan into the land that the LORD our God is giving us.’ But Sihon king of Heshbon refused to let us pass through his land, because the LORD your God had hardened his spirit and made his heart stubborn, so that he could hand him over to you, as you see today.

The defeat of Sihon king of Heshbon

Then the LORD said to me, ‘Look, I have begun to hand Sihon and his land over to you. Start now to take possession, so that his land will be yours.’ Sihon came out with his whole army to fight us at Jahaz. The LORD our God handed him over to us, and we defeated him, his sons and all his army. At that time we captured all his towns and devoted every one of them to destruction, with their men, women and children. We did not leave a single survivor. We took only the livestock as plunder for ourselves, along with the spoil from the towns we had captured. From Aroer, which stands at the edge of the Arnon Valley, and the town that lies in the valley, as far as Gilead, not a single town stood too high for us to take. The LORD our God gave every one of them over to us. But you did not go near the land of the Ammonites, the whole region along the Jabbok River and the towns in the hill country, just as the LORD our God had commanded.

fields.title: Deuteronomy 3
fields.body_html:
The defeat of Og king of Bashan

Then we turned and went up along the road to Bashan, and Og king of Bashan came out against us with all his army to do battle at Edrei. The LORD said to me, ‘Do not be afraid of him, for I have handed him over to you, together with all his army and his land. Treat him as you treated Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon.’ So the LORD our God handed Og king of Bashan and all his army over to us as well, and we struck him down until not one survivor was left to him. At that time we captured all his towns. There was not a single town we failed to take from them: sixty towns, the whole region of Argob, Og’s kingdom in Bashan. Every one of these towns was fortified with high walls and with barred double gates, and there were very many open villages besides. We devoted them to destruction, as we had done to Sihon king of Heshbon, devoting every town to destruction, men, women and children. The livestock, though, and the goods taken from the towns we kept as plunder for ourselves. So at that time we took the land of the two Amorite kings across the Jordan, from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon. (The Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, and the Amorites call it Senir.) We captured every town of the plateau, the whole of Gilead and the whole of Bashan, as far as Salecah and Edrei, towns that belonged to Og’s kingdom in Bashan. (Og king of Bashan was the only one left of the remnant of the Rephaim. His bed was made of iron, and it can still be seen in Rabbah of the Ammonites. It is about 13 1/2 feet long and 6 feet wide.) When we took possession of this land at that time, I gave to the Reubenites and the Gadites the stretch from Aroer beside the Arnon Valley, and half of the hill country of Gilead with its towns. To the half-tribe of Manasseh I gave the rest of Gilead and the whole of Bashan, the kingdom of Og. (The whole region of Argob, with all of Bashan, is known as a land of the Rephaim. Jair, of the line of Manasseh, took all the region of Argob up to the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and he gave these places in Bashan his own name, Havvoth-jair, which they still bear today.) To Machir I gave Gilead. To the Reubenites and the Gadites I gave the land that runs from Gilead to the Arnon Valley, its boundary running down the center of the valley, and on to the Jabbok River, the boundary of the Ammonites, and also the Arabah, with the Jordan as its border, from Chinnereth down to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, below the slopes of Pisgah on the east. At that time I gave you this command: ‘The LORD your God has given you this land to possess. But every fighting man among you is to cross over armed, going ahead of your fellow Israelites. Only your wives and children and your livestock — and I know how much livestock you have — are to stay behind in the towns I have given you, until the LORD grants your fellow Israelites rest, as he has granted it to you, and they in turn take possession of the land the LORD your God is giving them across the Jordan. Only then may each of you go back to the holding I have given you.’ At that time I commanded Joshua: ‘Your own eyes have seen everything the LORD your God did to these two kings. The LORD will deal in the same way with every kingdom you are crossing over to. Do not be afraid of them. The one who fights for you is the LORD your God himself.’

Moses pleads to cross the Jordan

At that time I pleaded with the LORD for his favor, saying, ‘Lord GOD, you have only begun to show your servant your greatness and your strong hand. Is there any god in heaven or on earth who can match your works and your mighty deeds? Please let me go across and see the good land on the far side of the Jordan, this good hill country and the Lebanon.’ But the LORD was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me. The LORD said to me, ‘Let that be enough! Do not bring this matter up with me again. Climb to the summit of Pisgah and look out to the west, the north, the south and the east. See the land with your own eyes, because you will not cross this Jordan. Instead, commission Joshua. Encourage him and give him strength, for he will cross over at the head of this people, and he will give them as their inheritance the land that you will see.’ So we stayed in the valley opposite Beth-peor.

fields.title: Deuteronomy 4
fields.body_html:
Listen to the statutes and rulings

Now, Israel, listen to the statutes and rulings that I am teaching you to put into practice. Then you will live, and you will enter and take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your ancestors, is giving you. Add nothing to the word I am commanding you, and take nothing away from it, so that you keep the commandments of the LORD your God that I am giving you. Your own eyes have seen what the LORD did at Baal-peor: every man who went after the Baal of Peor, the LORD your God wiped out from among you. But you who clung to the LORD your God are alive today, every one of you. See, I have taught you statutes and rulings, as the LORD my God commanded me, for you to live by in the land you are going into to take possession of. Keep them and follow them, for that is what will make you wise and understanding in the eyes of the peoples. When they hear about all these statutes, they will say, ‘This great nation is truly a wise and understanding people.’ For what great nation has gods as near to it as the LORD our God is to us whenever we call to him? And what great nation has statutes and rulings as righteous as this whole law that I put before you today? Only guard yourself and keep close watch over your life, so that you do not forget what your own eyes have seen, and so that it does not leave your mind for as long as you live. Make it known to your children and your grandchildren, above all the day you stood before the LORD your God at Horeb, when the LORD said to me, ‘Gather the people to me, and I will let them hear my words. Then they will learn to fear me as long as they live on the earth, and they will teach their children to do the same.’ You drew near and stood at the base of the mountain. It was burning with fire up into the heart of the sky, wrapped in darkness, cloud, and deep gloom. Then the LORD spoke to you out of the fire. You heard words being spoken, but you saw no form at all, only a voice. He made known to you his covenant, the Ten Words, which he commanded you to keep, and he wrote them on two stone tablets. At that time the LORD commanded me to teach you statutes and rulings for you to follow in the land you are crossing over to take possession of. Be very careful, then, for your own sake. On the day the LORD spoke to you at Horeb from the fire, you did not see any shape at all, so do not bring ruin on yourselves by making an idol for yourselves in the form of any figure, the likeness of a man or a woman, the likeness of any beast on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies through the sky, the likeness of anything that creeps on the ground, the likeness of any fish in the waters beneath the land. Do not raise your eyes to the sky and, seeing the sun, the moon, and the stars, all the host of heaven, be drawn away to bow down to them and serve them. The LORD your God has allotted them to all the peoples under the whole sky. But you are the ones the LORD took and brought out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be his own people, his inheritance, as you are today. Because of you, the LORD was angry with me and swore that I would not go over the Jordan or come into the good land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance. I must die here in this land and not cross the Jordan, but you are going over, and you will take possession of this good land. Watch yourselves, so that you do not forget the covenant the LORD your God made with you by making yourselves an idol shaped like anything at all, which the LORD your God has forbidden you. For the LORD your God is a devouring fire, a God who is jealous.

If you make an idol in the land

When you have had children and grandchildren and have grown old in the land, and you act corruptly and make an idol in the form of anything, doing what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God and provoking him to anger, Today I call heaven and earth to testify against you: you will soon be wiped out from the land you are crossing the Jordan to take possession of. You will not live long in it; you will be utterly destroyed. The LORD will scatter you among the peoples, and you will be left a small number among the nations to which the LORD drives you. There you will serve gods that human hands have made, wood and stone, gods that neither see nor hear, neither eat nor smell. But from there you will seek the LORD your God, and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul. In your distress, when all these things have overtaken you in the days to come, you will turn back to the LORD your God and obey him. For the LORD your God is a God of compassion. He will not let you go or bring you to ruin, and he will not forget the covenant he swore to your ancestors. Go ahead and inquire about the past, the days that came before you, back to the day God created human beings on the earth. Search from one edge of the sky to the other. Has anything this great ever taken place? Has anything like it ever been heard? Did any people ever hear the voice of God speaking from the midst of fire, as you heard it, and live? Or did any god ever attempt to come and take one nation for himself from within another, by trials, signs and wonders, by war, by a strong hand and an outstretched arm, and by great terrors, as the LORD your God did for you in Egypt while you watched? You were shown all this so that you would know that the LORD is God, and that there is no other besides him. He let you hear his voice from heaven to instruct you, and on earth he let you see his great fire; out of that fire you heard his words. He loved your ancestors and chose their descendants after them, and for that reason he himself brought you out of Egypt with his great power, driving out ahead of you nations bigger and mightier than you, to bring you in and give you their land as your inheritance, as it now is. So know this today, and take it to heart: the LORD is God in the heavens above and on the earth below, and there is no other. Keep his statutes and his commandments that I command you today, and things will go well for you and for your children after you, and you will have long life in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for all time.”

Three cities across the Jordan

Then Moses set apart three cities across the Jordan, to the east, so that anyone who had killed a neighbor by accident, without having been an enemy beforehand, could flee there. By fleeing to one of these cities, that person could stay alive. They were Bezer in the wilderness on the plateau, for the Reubenites; Ramoth in Gilead, for the Gadites; and Golan in Bashan, for the Manassites. This is the law that Moses laid before the Israelites. These are the decrees, statutes, and rulings that Moses spoke to the Israelites after they came out of Egypt, across the Jordan in the valley opposite Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon. Moses and the Israelites defeated him after they came out of Egypt. They took possession of his land and of the land of Og king of Bashan, those two kings of the Amorites who ruled across the Jordan, toward the sunrise, from Aroer on the edge of the Arnon Valley as far as Mount Siyon, that is, Hermon, and all the Arabah across the Jordan to the east, as far as the Sea of the Arabah, below the slopes of Pisgah.

fields.title: Deuteronomy 5
fields.body_html:
The Ten Words

Moses summoned all Israel and said to them, “Hear, Israel, the statutes and rulings that I am announcing to you today. Learn them and be careful to do them. The LORD our God made a covenant with us at Horeb. The LORD did not make this covenant with our fathers; he made it with us, the ones here today, all of us still alive. On the mountain the LORD spoke with you face to face, out of the fire. I was standing between the LORD and you at that time, to make known to you the word of the LORD, since you were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain. He said:

‘I am the LORD your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house where you were slaves. You shall have no other gods besides me. You shall not make yourself a carved idol in the form of anything in the heavens overhead, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth. You shall neither bow to them nor serve them. For I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God. I bring the guilt of fathers upon their children, upon the third and the fourth generation of those who hate me, but to thousands who love me and keep my commandments I show faithful love.

You shall not use the name of the LORD your God for what is false or worthless, for the LORD will not let anyone go unpunished who uses his name that way.

Keep the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy, as the LORD your God commanded you. You have six days to labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath for the LORD your God. Do no work on it: not you, nor your son or daughter, nor your male or female servant, nor your ox or your donkey or any of your livestock, nor the foreigner living among you in your towns, so that your male and female servants may rest as you do. Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD your God led you out from there by a strong hand and an outstretched arm. For this reason the LORD your God has commanded you to observe the Sabbath day. Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God has commanded you. Then your days will be long, and it will go well with you in the land the LORD your God is going to give you.

You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not give baseless evidence against your neighbor.

You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. You shall not crave your neighbor’s house, his field, his male or female servant, his ox or his donkey, or anything else your neighbor has.’

Out of the fire

The LORD spoke these words to your whole assembly at the mountain, in a great voice out of the fire, the cloud and the thick darkness, and he said no more. He wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to me. When you heard the voice coming out of the darkness and the mountain was burning with fire, all your tribal heads and your elders came near to me, and you said, ‘The LORD our God has shown us his glory and his greatness, and we have heard his voice out of the fire. Today we have seen that God may speak with a person, and that person may still live. So why should we die now? This great fire will devour us. If we go on hearing the voice of the LORD our God, we will die. Of all mortals, who has heard the voice of the living God speak from the fire as we have, and stayed alive? You go near and hear all that the LORD our God says, and then you tell us all that the LORD our God tells you; we will listen and do it.’ The LORD heard what you said when you spoke to me, and the LORD said to me, ‘I have heard what this people said to you. They have spoken well in everything they said. If only their hearts would stay like this, so that they would fear me and keep all my commandments always, and it would go well with them and with their children forever! Go and tell them, “Go back to your tents.” But you, stay here with me, and I will tell you the whole commandment, the statutes and the rulings that you are to teach them, so that they may do them in the land I am giving them to take possession of.’ Take care, then, to do just as the LORD your God has commanded you, turning neither to the right nor to the left. Walk in every part of the way that the LORD your God has commanded you. Then you will live, it will be well with you, and your days will be long in the land you are going to take possession of.

fields.title: Deuteronomy 6
fields.body_html:
Hear, Israel

This is the commandment, the statutes and rulings, that the LORD your God commanded me to teach you, so that you will keep them in the land you are crossing over to take possession of, so that you may fear the LORD your God and keep all his statutes and commandments that I am giving you, you and your children and grandchildren, as long as you live, and so that your life may be long. Listen then, Israel, and keep them with care. Then all will be well with you, and you will become very many in a land flowing with milk and honey, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you.

Hear, Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. You are to love the LORD your God with your whole heart, with your whole being, and with all your strength. Keep these words that I am commanding you today close to your heart. Teach them carefully to your children, and speak of them as you sit in your house and as you go on your way, as you lie down and as you rise. Tie them as a sign on your hand, and let them be a band between your eyes. Write them on the doorposts of your house and on the gates of your town.

Do not forget the LORD

The LORD your God is bringing you into the land he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, that he would give you. It has great and fine cities that you did not build, houses full of every kind of good thing that you did not put in them, cisterns cut in the rock that you did not cut, vineyards and olive groves you did not plant. When you have eaten your fill, then watch yourself, so that you do not forget the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. Fear the LORD your God and no other; serve him, and swear your oaths by his name. You must not go after other gods, any of the gods of the peoples that surround you. For the LORD your God, who is in your midst, is a jealous God; beware, or the anger of the LORD your God will blaze against you and he will wipe you off the face of the earth.

You must not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah. Take care to keep the commandments of the LORD your God, his decrees and his statutes, which he has commanded you. Do what the LORD sees as right and good, so that all will be well with you and you can enter and take possession of the good land that the LORD swore to your fathers, driving out all your enemies before you, as the LORD promised.

When your son asks you

Some day your son will ask you, ‘What do they mean, these decrees, statutes and rulings that the LORD our God has commanded you?’ Then tell your son, ‘In Egypt we were slaves to Pharaoh, but by his strong hand the LORD led us out of Egypt. We saw it with our own eyes: the LORD brought great and devastating signs and wonders on Egypt, on Pharaoh and on all his household. Us, though, he led out from there, so that he could bring us in and give us the land he swore to our fathers. The LORD commanded us to keep all these statutes and to fear the LORD our God, for our good always, so that he might keep us alive, as we are today. Righteousness will be ours if we take care to keep this whole commandment in the presence of the LORD our God, as he commanded us.’

fields.title: Deuteronomy 7
fields.body_html:
The nations in the land

When the LORD your God brings you into the land you are about to enter and take as your own, and clears many nations out of your way, the Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, seven nations greater in number and might than you, and when the LORD your God hands them over to you and you defeat them, then you are to devote them wholly to destruction. Make no covenant with them, and grant them no favor. Do not join your families to theirs by marriage: your daughters are not to marry their sons, nor are your sons to take their daughters as wives. For they would draw your sons away from following me, into the service of other gods, and then the anger of the LORD would flare up against you and he would soon destroy you. Instead, deal with them in this way: pull down their altars, break their standing stones to pieces, cut down their Asherah poles, and burn their carved images. You are a people set apart as holy to the LORD your God. From among every people on the face of the earth, the LORD your God picked you out to belong to him as his treasured possession.

The LORD chose you

The LORD gave his heart to you and chose you, not because there were more of you than of any other people, for you were the smallest of all the peoples, but because the LORD loved you and would not break the oath he swore to your ancestors. So he led you out by his strong hand and bought you free from the house where you were slaves, out of the grip of Pharaoh king of Egypt. So understand that the LORD your God is the true God, the faithful God. He keeps his covenant and his faithful love for a thousand generations with those who love him and keep his commandments, but he repays those who hate him, each one in person, and destroys them. He does not put off dealing with anyone who hates him; he repays that person directly. So keep the commandment, the statutes and the rulings that I am giving you today, and carry them out.

If you listen to these rulings and keep them and carry them out, then in return the LORD your God will keep with you the covenant and the faithful love he promised your ancestors on oath. He will love you, bless you and make you numerous. He will bless the children you bear and the harvest of your soil, your grain, your new wine and your olive oil, and the young of your cattle and your sheep, in the land he promised on oath to your ancestors to give you. Of all peoples, you will be the most blessed. Among you there will be no man or woman unable to have children, and among your animals none that bears no young. The LORD will keep every sickness away from you. None of the dreadful diseases of Egypt that you came to know will he bring on you; instead, he will put them on all who hate you. You are to make an end of all the peoples the LORD your God is handing over to you. Let no pity for them hold you back, and do not serve their gods; that would be a trap to catch you.

Do not be afraid of these nations

Perhaps you will think to yourself, ‘These nations outnumber us. How could we ever drive them out?’ Do not fear them. Keep firmly in mind what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and the whole of Egypt, the great trials that you watched with your own eyes, the signs, the wonders, the strong hand and the outstretched arm by which the LORD your God led you out. That is what the LORD your God will do to every people you are afraid of. What is more, the LORD your God will send the hornet against them, until even those left alive and in hiding from you are gone. Do not tremble before them. The LORD your God is there among you, a God great and awe-inspiring. The LORD your God will clear these nations out of your way a little at a time. You will not be able to finish them off all at once, or the wild animals would become too many for you. The LORD your God will hand them over to you and throw them into great panic until they are wiped out. He will put their kings in your power, and you will blot their name out from under heaven. No one will hold out against you until you have destroyed them. Burn the carved images of their gods in the fire. Do not set your heart on the silver or gold that covers them, and do not carry it off for yourself; it would catch you like a trap, for the LORD your God detests it. Do not bring anything detestable into your home; if you do, you will become a devoted thing just as it is, marked for destruction. Loathe it and detest it with all your being, for it is a devoted thing.

fields.title: Deuteronomy 8
fields.body_html:
Remember the journey in the wilderness

Be careful to carry out every commandment that I am giving you today, so that you may live and grow in number, and go in and take possession of the land that the LORD promised on oath to your ancestors. Remember the whole journey on which the LORD your God led you these forty years in the wilderness. He did it to humble you and to test you, to know what was in your heart: would you keep his commandments or not? He brought you low and let you go hungry, then gave you manna to eat, a food that neither you nor your ancestors had ever known. He did this to teach you that people do not live on bread alone, but people live on everything that comes from the mouth of the LORD. The clothes on your back did not wear out, and your feet did not swell, all these forty years. So understand in your heart that the LORD your God disciplines you just as a father disciplines his son. Keep the commandments of the LORD your God, living by his ways and holding him in awe. For the LORD your God is bringing you into a good land, a land with flowing streams, with springs and underground waters that pour out in the valleys and the hills, a land of wheat and barley, of vines, fig trees and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey, a land where you will eat food without shortage and lack nothing, a land whose rocks hold iron and from whose hills you can dig copper. When you have eaten and are full, you are to bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you. Be on your guard against forgetting the LORD your God by neglecting his commandments, his rulings and his statutes that I am giving you today, otherwise, when you have eaten your fill and have built fine houses and live in them, and when your herds and flocks grow large, and your silver and gold increase, and everything you own multiplies, your heart may grow proud and you may forget the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, who guided you through that vast and dreadful wilderness, a land of fiery snakes and scorpions, of parched ground without water, who made water come out of flint rock for you, who gave you manna to eat in the wilderness, a food unknown to your ancestors, so as to humble you and test you and in the end to bring you good, and you may say to yourself, ‘My own power and the strength of my own hands have won me this wealth.’ Remember the LORD your God instead. It is he who gives you the ability to grow wealthy, in order to carry out the covenant he swore to your ancestors, as he is doing today.

If you forget the LORD

If you ever do forget the LORD your God and follow other gods, serving them and bowing down to them, I declare to you today, as a witness, that you will certainly perish. Like the nations that the LORD is destroying ahead of you, so you will perish, because you would not obey the LORD your God.

fields.title: Deuteronomy 9
fields.body_html:
Not because you are righteous

Hear, Israel: today you are about to cross the Jordan, to go in and drive out nations greater and stronger than you, with great cities fortified up to the sky, a people strong and tall, the Anakim. You know about them, and you have heard it said, ‘Who can stand up to the descendants of Anak?’ So understand today that the LORD your God is the one who goes across ahead of you like a consuming fire. He will destroy them and bring them down before you, and you will drive them out and wipe them out quickly, as the LORD promised you. When the LORD your God has pushed them out of your way, do not tell yourself, ‘It is because I am righteous that the LORD has brought me in to take possession of this land.’ No, it is because of the wickedness of these nations that the LORD is driving them out before you. It is not because you are righteous or because your heart is upright that you are going in to take possession of their land. It is because of the wickedness of these nations that the LORD your God is driving them out before you, and to keep the promise that the LORD made on oath to your ancestors, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Understand, then, that it is not because you are righteous that the LORD your God is giving you this good land to possess, for you are a stiff-necked people. Remember this and never forget it: how you made the LORD your God angry in the wilderness. From the day you left the land of Egypt until you arrived here, you have kept on rebelling against the LORD. Even at Horeb you provoked the LORD to anger, and the LORD was so angry with you that he was ready to destroy you. When I went up the mountain to receive the stone tablets, the tablets of the covenant that the LORD made with you, I stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights without eating food or drinking water. The LORD gave me the two stone tablets written by the finger of God. On them were all the words the LORD had spoken to you on the mountain out of the fire, on the day of the assembly. At the end of the forty days and forty nights, the LORD gave me the two stone tablets, the tablets of the covenant. Then the LORD said to me, ‘Get up and go down from here at once, because your people whom you brought out of Egypt have become corrupt. They have been quick to turn from the way I commanded them; they have made themselves an idol of cast metal.’ The LORD also said to me, ‘I have seen this people, and they are indeed a stiff-necked people. Leave me alone, so that I can destroy them and wipe out their name from under heaven. Then I will make you into a nation stronger and larger than they are.’ So I turned and went down from the mountain while it was blazing with fire, with the two tablets of the covenant in my hands. I looked, and there it was: you had sinned against the LORD your God. You had made yourselves a calf cast in metal. You had been quick to turn from the way the LORD had commanded you. So I seized the two tablets, threw them down from my hands, and smashed them before your eyes. Then I lay face down before the LORD as I had the first time, for forty days and forty nights, without eating food or drinking water, because of all the sin you had committed by doing what was evil in the sight of the LORD and provoking him to anger. I was terrified of the anger and fury the LORD felt against you, enough to destroy you. But the LORD listened to me that time too. The LORD was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him, and at that time I prayed for Aaron as well. Then I took the sinful thing you had made, the calf, and burned it in the fire. I crushed it and ground it thoroughly until it was as fine as dust, and I threw the dust into the stream that flows down the mountain. At Taberah, at Massah, and at Kibroth-hattaavah you also made the LORD angry. And when the LORD sent you out from Kadesh-barnea and said, ‘Go up and take possession of the land I have given you,’ you rebelled against the command of the LORD your God. You did not trust him or obey him. You have been rebelling against the LORD from the day I first knew you. So I lay face down before the LORD those forty days and forty nights, because the LORD had said he would destroy you. I prayed to the LORD and said, ‘Lord GOD, do not destroy your people, your own inheritance, whom you redeemed by your great power and brought out of Egypt with a mighty hand. Remember your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Do not look at the stubbornness of this people, or at their wickedness and their sin, Otherwise the people of the land you brought us out of will say, “Because the LORD could not bring them into the land he had promised them, and because he hated them, he led them out to kill them in the wilderness.” Yet they are your people, your inheritance, whom you brought out by your great power and your outstretched arm.’

fields.title: Deuteronomy 10
fields.body_html:
The two new stone tablets

At that time the LORD said to me, ‘Cut two stone tablets like the first ones and come up to me on the mountain, and make a wooden ark for yourself, and I will write on these tablets the words that were on the first tablets, the ones you broke. Then put them in the ark.’ So I made an ark of acacia wood, cut two tablets of stone like the first, and climbed the mountain carrying the two tablets. Then he wrote on the tablets what had been written before: the Ten Words that the LORD spoke to you on the mountain out of the fire on the day the assembly gathered. And the LORD gave them to me. Then I turned and came down from the mountain and put the tablets in the ark I had made. They are still there, just as the LORD commanded me. The Israelites set out from Beeroth Bene-jaakan for Moserah. There Aaron died and was buried, and his son Eleazar became priest in his place. From there they set out for Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah for Jotbathah, a land of flowing streams. It was then that the LORD set the tribe of Levi apart: to carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD, to stand before the LORD and serve him, and to bless in his name. They do so to this day. For this reason Levi has been given no portion of land, no inheritance among his brothers; the LORD is his inheritance, just as the LORD your God promised him. As before, I remained on the mountain for forty days and forty nights, and this time too the LORD heard me; he was not willing to destroy you. Then the LORD said to me, ‘Get up and set out at the head of the people, so that they may go in and take possession of the land I swore to their ancestors to give them.’

What the LORD asks of you

And now, Israel, what is it that the LORD your God asks of you? Just this: that you fear the LORD your God, follow all his ways and love him, and that you serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and that you keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD that I am giving you today, for your own good. See, the LORD your God owns the heavens, even the highest heavens, along with the earth and all that it holds. Even so, it was your ancestors that the LORD was drawn to in love, and after them he chose their offspring, you, from among all the peoples, as is plain today. Circumcise your hearts, then, and stop stiffening your necks. For the LORD your God is God over all gods and Lord over all lords. He is the great God, mighty and awe-inspiring, who plays no favorites and cannot be moved by a bribe. He sees that orphans and widows get justice, and he loves the outsider living among you and gives them food and clothing. You too must love the outsider, since you were outsiders yourselves in the land of Egypt. It is the LORD your God you must fear and serve; hold fast to him, and swear your oaths by his name. He is the one you praise and he is your God. You have seen with your own eyes the great and awe-inspiring deeds he has done for you. Your ancestors were seventy persons when they went down to Egypt, and now the LORD your God has made you like the stars of the heavens, past counting.

fields.title: Deuteronomy 11
fields.body_html:
Love the LORD your God

So love the LORD your God, and always keep his requirements, his statutes, his rulings, and his commandments. Recognize today — for it is not your children I am speaking to, who have neither known nor seen it — the discipline of the LORD your God: his greatness, his mighty hand and his outstretched arm, his signs and the deeds he did in Egypt to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his whole land, what he did to the Egyptian army, its horses and its chariots, how he made the waters of the Red Sea flow over them as they chased you, and the LORD destroyed them, and they are gone to this day, what he did for you in the wilderness until you arrived at this place, and what he did to Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab son of Reuben, when the earth opened its mouth in the middle of all Israel and swallowed them, with their households, their tents, and every living thing that belonged to them, for it is your own eyes that have seen all the great work that the LORD has done. So keep the whole commandment that I am giving you today, so that you may have strength to go in and take possession of the land you are crossing over to possess, and so that you may live long in the land that the LORD swore to your ancestors to give to them and to their descendants, a land flowing with milk and honey.

A land that drinks in the rain

For the land you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt that you came out of, where you sowed your seed and watered it by foot, like a vegetable garden. But the land you are crossing over to possess is a land of hills and valleys, which drinks in water from the rain of the sky, a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are on it always, from the beginning of the year to its end.

If you truly obey my commandments that I am giving you today, loving the LORD your God and serving him with all your heart and with all your soul, then I will give your land its rain at the right time, the autumn rain and the spring rain, and you will gather in your grain, your new wine, and your olive oil. I will provide grass in your fields for your livestock, and you will eat and be full. Be careful that your hearts are not led astray, so that you turn away and serve other gods and bow down to them, and the anger of the LORD blaze against you. Then he will shut up the sky so that there is no rain and the ground yields no crops, and you will quickly be wiped out from the good land that the LORD is giving you. Fix these words of mine in your heart and in your soul. Tie them as a sign on your hand, and let them be a band between your eyes. Teach them to your children, talking about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. Write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates, so that you and your children may live long in the land the LORD swore to your ancestors to give them, as long as the sky remains above the earth.

For if you carefully keep this whole commandment that I am giving you to follow, loving the LORD your God, walking in all his ways, and holding fast to him, then the LORD will drive out all these nations ahead of you, and you will dispossess nations greater and stronger than you are. Every place where you set foot will be yours. Your territory will reach from the wilderness to Lebanon, and from the River, the Euphrates, to the western sea. No one will be able to stand against you. The LORD your God will put the dread and fear of you on the whole land where you set foot, as he promised you.

A blessing and a curse

See, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse: the blessing if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God that I am giving you today, and the curse if you do not obey the commandments of the LORD your God, but turn aside from the way I am commanding you today and follow other gods that you have not known.

When the LORD your God brings you into the land you are entering to possess, you are to proclaim the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. Are they not across the Jordan, beyond the road toward the sunset, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the Arabah, facing Gilgal, beside the oaks of Moreh? For you are about to cross the Jordan to go in and take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you. When you have taken possession of it and are living in it, be careful to carry out all the statutes and rulings that I am setting before you today.

fields.title: Deuteronomy 12
fields.body_html:
The place the LORD will choose

These are the statutes and rulings you must be careful to keep in the land that the LORD, the God of your ancestors, has given you to possess, for as long as you live on its soil. You must completely destroy all the places where the nations you are driving out worshiped their gods, on the high mountains, on the hills, and under every leafy tree. Tear down their altars, smash their sacred stones, burn their Asherah poles, cut down the carved images of their gods, and wipe out their name from that place. You must not worship the LORD your God in that way. Instead, you must seek the place that the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name there as his dwelling, and go there. Bring there your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the gifts you set apart, your vow offerings and your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herds and flocks. There you and your households are to eat in the presence of the LORD your God and rejoice in all that you have set your hand to, all that the LORD your God has blessed you with. You must not do as we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever seems right to them, because you have not yet reached the place of rest, the inheritance that the LORD your God is giving you. But you will cross the Jordan and settle in the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance. He will give you rest from all the enemies around you, and you will live in safety, then you are to bring everything I am commanding you to the place that the LORD your God will choose as a dwelling for his name: your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the gifts you set apart, and all the fine offerings you vow to the LORD. And you shall rejoice in the presence of the LORD your God, you and your sons and daughters, your male and female servants, and the Levite who lives in your towns, since he has no share or inheritance among you. Be careful not to offer your burnt offerings at any place you happen to see, but only at the place that the LORD will choose in one of your tribes. There you are to offer your burnt offerings, and there you are to do everything I am commanding you. However, you may slaughter and eat meat in any of your towns whenever you wish, as much as the LORD your God has blessed you with. Both those who are ritually unclean and those who are clean may eat it, as they would a gazelle or a deer. But you must not eat the blood; pour it out on the ground like water. You may not eat in your own towns the tithe of your grain, new wine and oil, or the firstborn of your herds and flocks, or any of the offerings you vow, or your freewill offerings, or the gifts you set apart, but you are to eat them in the presence of the LORD your God, at the place that the LORD your God will choose, you and your son and daughter, your male and female servants, and the Levite who lives in your towns. Rejoice there before the LORD your God in all that you have set your hand to. Be careful not to neglect the Levite as long as you live in your land.

Eating meat in your towns

When the LORD your God enlarges your territory as he promised you, and you say, ‘I want to eat some meat,’ because you are longing for meat, you may eat meat whenever you want. If the place where the LORD your God chooses to put his name is too far from you, you may slaughter animals from the herds and flocks that the LORD has given you, as I have commanded you, and eat them in your own towns whenever you wish. Eat it just as a gazelle or a deer is eaten; those who are ritually unclean and those who are clean may eat it alike. Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, because the blood is the life, and you must not eat the life with the meat. Do not eat it; pour it out on the ground like water. Do not eat it, so that all may go well with you and your children after you, because you will be doing what is right in the sight of the LORD. But take your holy offerings that are due from you and your vow offerings, and go with them to the place that the LORD will choose. Offer your burnt offerings, both meat and blood, on the altar of the LORD your God. The blood of your other sacrifices is to be poured out on the altar of the LORD your God, but you may eat the meat. Be careful to obey all these words I am commanding you, so that all may go well with you and your children after you forever, because you will be doing what is good and right in the sight of the LORD your God.

Do not follow the ways of the nations

When the LORD your God cuts off before you the nations you are going in to drive out, and you drive them out and settle in their land, be careful not to be trapped into following them after they have been destroyed before you. Do not ask about their gods, saying, ‘How did these nations worship their gods? I will do the same.’ You must not worship the LORD your God in that way, because for their gods they have done every detestable thing that the LORD hates. They even burn their sons and daughters in the fire as offerings to their gods. Be careful to do everything I command you. Do not add to it or take anything away from it.

fields.title: Deuteronomy 13
fields.body_html:
A prophet or dreamer who urges other gods

Suppose a prophet or someone who has dreams appears among you and announces to you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or wonder he told you about comes true, and he says, ‘Let us follow other gods’—gods you have not known—‘and let us worship them,’ you must not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer. The LORD your God is testing you, to find out whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul. It is the LORD your God you must follow, and him you must fear. Keep his commandments, listen to his voice, serve him, and hold fast to him. That prophet or dreamer must be put to death, because he has urged rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery. He has tried to turn you aside from the way the LORD your God commanded you to walk in. You must purge the evil from among you. If your own brother, your mother’s son, or your son or your daughter, or the wife you embrace, or the friend who is as dear to you as your own life, secretly entices you, saying, ‘Let us go and worship other gods’—gods that neither you nor your ancestors have known, any of the gods of the peoples around you, whether near you or far from you, from one end of the earth to the other, you must not give in to them or listen to them. Show them no pity, do not spare them, and do not cover up for them, but you must certainly put them to death. Your hand must be the first raised against them to put them to death, and then the hands of all the people. Stone them to death, because they tried to draw you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. Then all Israel will hear and be afraid, and no one among you will ever again do such an evil thing.

A town that turns to other gods

If you hear it said about one of the towns the LORD your God is giving you to live in that some worthless men have come out from among you and have led the people of their town astray, saying, ‘Let us go and worship other gods’—gods you have not known— then you must look into it, search it out, and ask thorough questions. If it is true and the matter is certain that this detestable thing has been done among you, you must put the people who live in that town to the sword. Devote it to destruction, with everything in it and its livestock, putting them to the sword. Gather all its plunder into the middle of its public square, and burn the town and all its plunder with fire as a whole offering to the LORD your God. It must remain a ruin mound forever and never be rebuilt.
